newsitem.title: UK: FOCUS - UK manufacturing rebounds, services soften.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - UK manufacturing rebounds, services soften.

text.p: British manufacturing output staged a modest rebound in June after falling unexpectedly in May, but the services sector, the main engine of the economic boom, grew at a slightly slower rate in July.

Although the figures provided little evidence that the economy was overheating, economists said the Bank of England's Monetary Policy Committee was still likely to raise interest rates for the fourth month in a row on Thursday to dampen rampant consumer spending.

The Office for National Statistics (ONS) said manufacturing output rose 0.4 percent in June after an unexpected fall of one percent in May, and was up 1.2 percent year-on-year. However, output fell 0.1 percent in the second quarter compared with the first quarter.

"The pound's strength is clearly dampening the demand for UK goods in overseas markets and there must be a real danger of a further fall in output in the third quarter, putting manufacturing technically back into recession," said Jonathan Loynes, an economist at HSBC.

Overall industrial production was up 1.4 percent in June, way above market forecasts of a 0.5 percent rise, and expanded 1.9 percent year-on-year. The rise was largely due to higher oil and gas output.
Separately, the Chartered Institute of Purchasing and Supply said in its July report on the services sector that the strong pound was starting to hurt service providers as well as manufacturers.
Its monthly survey, sponsored by Reuters, showed the service sector continued to grow strongly but at a less vigorous pace than in recent months.

"Buoyant consumer confidence was again reported to have played a key role in boosting demand, but the July survey saw the first evidence of the strength of the pound damaging the competitiveness of UK service providers, resulting in a slight slowing in the rate of growth of new business," the institute said.

Another survey, by the Confederation of British Industry (CBI) and Business Strategies Ltd, showed optimism about export prospects over the coming year fell sharply among manufacturers in 10 out of 11 British regions in the four months to July.
"The high value of sterling is undoubtedly the primary cause of weaker exports," the CBI said.
"The regional picture in manufacturing reflects the situation in the national economy, where there is a clear divide between strengthening domestic demand and weaker exports."

Economists said Tuesday's figures did little to help resolve the dilemma facing the Bank of England's monetary policy committee, which was given freedom to set interest rates by the new Labour government in May.

The dilemma is that strong consumer spending, fuelled by around 35 billion pounds of "windfall" gains from building society flotations, appears to require higher interest rates if it is not to result in inflation.

However, higher rates would boost an already strong pound and risk tipping the struggling manufacturing sector into recession. Official rates have risen in three quarter-point steps since May to 6.75 percent.

"The official data suggest that the strength of the domestic economy might not be sufficiently strong to offset the continued weakness of exports," said economists Simon Briscoe and Edmund Nonis of Nikko Securities.
"The danger remains that further tightening of monetary policy and appreciation of sterling could stop the manufacturing in its tracks, threatening recession next year."
Andrew Cates, an economist at UBS, said he expected a quarter-point interest rate rise on Thursday but did not believe it was necessary.
"There has been little evidence during the past month which suggests that the wider economy is overheating and that the inflation target is in jeopardy," he said.
